content:
Joshua Wong was charged with conspiracy to collude with foreign forces together with Nathan Law and others in 2020. He pleaded guilty today (the 2nd) at the High Court. National security law designated judge Justice Tam Yiu-ho adjourned sentencing, saying he was aware that Wong was originally scheduled for release on January 7, 2027, and would set a sentencing date as soon as possible. Several former members of Scholarism, who had known Wong for over a decade, attended the hearing today to show support. After the court adjourned, Sharon Chin said she was not optimistic about the sentence, noting that Wong was active in his actions but would "definitely be under tremendous psychological and mental pressure." She also said friends who know him could continue to write letters, "so he knows there are still many people outside who care about him." Related reports: Joshua Wong Case | Charged with Conspiracy to Collude with Foreign Forces, Wong Pleads Guilty; Wong Has Been Deprived of Freedom for Over 2,100 Days, Charged with Conspiracy to Collude with Foreign Forces, to Enter Plea and Receive Sentence Tomorrow

Suspected queue placeholders deployed last night, court-watching supporters took the first seven spots

Last night, nearly 10 pm, nearly 40 people were already queuing on site, with the first seven being court-watching supporters who have been following Wong's case. The supporter at the front of the queue arrived around 5:30 pm, saying they hoped to enter the main courtroom to show support. By around 8 pm, several suspected queue placeholders arrived, and within less than 30 minutes, a large group of nearly 20 people arrived simultaneously to register the remaining main courtroom seats with the police. One court-watcher said that in previous hearings of Wong's case there had been no queue placeholders, "last time our friends filled three-quarters of the courtroom," describing the situation as unusual.

Jimmy Sham, one of the 47 defendants released, attended the hearing today.

Sharon Chin said Wong was very active in his actions, but she believed he must be facing psychological and mental pressure.

Chin Pui-man not optimistic about sentence, says Wong is under psychological pressure

Former Scholarism member Sharon Chin, visibly pregnant, attended the hearing. After the court adjourned, when asked by reporters how she felt, she said "the pressure is considerable," noting that for the sentence there was only the Jimmy Lai case for reference, "so I wouldn't say I'm too optimistic that it will be a very short sentence." Over the past few years, she has visited Wong in prison regularly, saying he "is psychologically prepared," exercises daily, reads books, describing him as "active in his actions, but psychologically or mentally there will definitely be great pressure." She said she would visit and write to Wong regularly to support him, and added "if you all know him, you can continue to write to him, so he knows there are still many people outside who care about him."

Former Scholarism member Louis (right), who has visited Wong at Stanley Prison every month for the past five years, said he has been working hard to discover new interests and things.

Louis: He continues to work hard discovering new interests and things

Former Scholarism member Louis attended the hearing; he has visited Wong at Stanley Prison every month for the past five years. He said he had known Wong for over a decade. Wong was originally scheduled for release in January 2027, but was charged again in this case. Although it was expected, he still felt sad: "after all, no one wants to spend even one extra day in prison." However, he noted that Wong has been studying and reading diligently in prison, "doing his own daily things," such as playing guitar and working out, constantly striving to discover new interests and things. "I hope everyone can learn from him in this regard, and continue to maintain their own daily lives." Beyond continuing to attend the hearings, he would also continue to do his own part well.

Regarding the sentence, Louis said it was hard to judge, but as a friend he "hopes it will be as short as possible." When asked if there was anything he wanted to say to Wong, he said "I believe that both I and he, or the friends outside, we will each do our own part well, and each continue to work hard in our own fields." As for suspected queue placeholders occupying the main courtroom seats, he said he longed for the chance to see Wong in the main courtroom, but felt it was impossible to prevent, "I think as long as everyone has done their best, that's enough." He also said he believed Wong has always felt everyone's support for him.

Candy: He is a person who truly loves Hong Kong

Former Scholarism member Candy said she had known Wong since 2013, when he was a very dedicated working partner, and since they were around the same age, they were "friends who would laugh and joke around." She said she has written to him in the past two or three years and visited him occasionally, describing his state as "sometimes quite good, sometimes not so good."

Candy estimated that Wong would be sentenced to over 10 years. She frankly said it was a bit of a pity, pointing out that people in their 20s and 30s "should be enjoying their lives, developing their careers, and spending time with family and friends," but instead have to spend a lot of time in prison. She said Wong has put in a lot of effort for Hong Kong's political development, and is "a person who truly loves Hong Kong." Although he may feel that he chose this path himself, as a friend, "I feel he deserves more time with his family and friends," and "as a person, he deserves the chance to be free." When asked if there was anything she wanted to say to Wong, Candy said: "I hope he's safe and healthy. Although he has to go through a period of time inside, maybe he'll get to know more friends. I hope he stays healthy and safe."

Former League of Social Democrats member Tsang Kin-ching said Wong has already served over 2,000 days, "I hope the sentence is short, and he can come out as soon as possible." When asked about his expected sentence, he said "you know with national security law judges you can never guess, the state calls the shots now, going from governance to prosperity, silence reigns."
